“You've stirred up an unnatural soul and spirit in him, ma'am, quite unsuitable for someone in his position. The board will tell you that, Mrs. Sowerberry; they're practical philosophers. What business do paupers have with souls or spirits? It's quite enough that we allow them to keep their bodies alive. If you'd kept the boy on thin porridge, ma'am, none of this would have happened.”

“Dear, dear!” Mrs. Sowerberry exclaimed, raising her eyes piously toward the kitchen ceiling. “This is what comes of generosity!”

Mrs. Sowerberry's generosity to Oliver had consisted of giving him large quantities of dirty scraps that nobody else would eat. It therefore showed great humility and self-sacrifice that she willingly accepted Mr. Bumble's serious accusation. To be fair to her, she was entirely innocent of generosity in thought, word, or deed.

“Ah!” said Mr. Bumble, once her eyes returned to earth. “The only thing to do now, as far as I can see, is leave him in the cellar for a day or two until hunger has quieted him down. Then take him out and feed him nothing but porridge for the rest of his apprenticeship. He comes from a bad family. Excitable people, Mrs. Sowerberry! Both the nurse and the doctor said his mother struggled here through hardship and pain that would have killed any properly behaved woman weeks earlier.”

Oliver heard just enough of this to realize they were speaking about his mother. He began kicking again, so violently that every other sound was drowned out. At that moment Sowerberry returned. The women explained Oliver's offense, adding whatever exaggerations they thought most likely to make him angry. He immediately unlocked the cellar door and hauled his rebellious apprentice out by the collar.

Oliver's clothes were torn from the beating he had received. His face was bruised and scratched, and his hair hung across his forehead. But his cheeks still burned with anger. As he was dragged out of his prison, he glared boldly at Noah, looking completely unafraid.

“Well, aren't you a fine young fellow?” said Sowerberry, shaking Oliver and slapping his ear.

“He insulted my mother,” Oliver replied.

“And what if he did, you ungrateful little wretch?” said Mrs. Sowerberry. “She deserved everything he said, and worse.”

“She didn't,” said Oliver.

“She did,” said Mrs. Sowerberry.

“That's a lie!” said Oliver.

Mrs. Sowerberry burst into tears.

Those tears left Mr. Sowerberry no choice. Any experienced reader will understand that, under all the established rules of married quarrels, even a moment's hesitation before punishing Oliver severely would have made him a brute, an unnatural husband, an insulting creature, a worthless imitation of a man, and various other pleasant things too numerous to fit into this chapter.

She now felt strongly tempted to go to the street door; she wished to discover whether it was raining. Why should she accuse herself of any other purpose? Captain Wentworth must already be out of view. She rose from her chair, determined to go. One part of her ought not always to be so much wiser than the other, or continually suspect it of being worse than it was. She would look at the rain. In an instant, however, she was driven back by Captain Wentworth's own entrance, accompanied by ladies and gentlemen who were plainly his acquaintances and whom he must have met a little below Milsom Street. At seeing her he appeared more visibly startled and disconcerted than she had ever known him; his face was quite flushed. For the first time since they had met again, she felt herself the less revealing of the two. Those last few moments of preparation gave her an advantage. The overwhelming, blinding confusion of the first surprise had already passed for her. Yet she still had more than enough to feel: agitation, hurt, pleasure, something poised between happiness and misery.

He addressed her and then turned aside. Embarrassment defined his manner. She could not have described it as cold or warm with anything like the certainty with which she could call it embarrassed.

After a brief pause, he approached and spoke once more. They exchanged questions on ordinary subjects, probably neither learning much from the answers, while Anne remained acutely aware that he was less comfortable than before. Through being so constantly together, they had learned to converse with a fair appearance of composure and indifference; now he could no longer manage it. Time had altered him, or Louisa had. Some kind of self-consciousness was at work. He looked very well, with no sign of injured health or spirits, and spoke of Uppercross, the Musgroves, even Louisa. When he mentioned her, his face briefly showed its old look of mischievous meaning. Yet this was still Captain Wentworth ill at ease, uncomfortable, and unable to pretend otherwise.

Anne was not surprised, but was hurt, to find that Elizabeth refused to acknowledge him. She saw that each had noticed the other and that both fully recognized their acquaintance. She felt certain he was prepared for a greeting, indeed expecting one, and she suffered as she watched her sister turn away with unyielding coldness.

Lady Dalrymple's carriage, whose delay was making Miss Elliot increasingly impatient, now arrived, and the servant entered to announce it.

“Certainly not,” Duff answered.

“And if I translate ‘yokel’ for the ladies' benefit, I take you to mean that no countryman made this attempt?” said Mr. Losberne, smiling.

“That's the meaning, master,” Blathers replied. “Is that everything about the robbery?”

“Everything,” said the doctor.

“Then what's this business about the boy the servants keep talking of?” Blathers asked.

“Nothing whatever,” the doctor replied. “One frightened servant has chosen to imagine that he was involved in this attempted break-in. But it's nonsense, complete absurdity.”

“Very easily settled, if that's so,” Duff observed.

“He's quite right there,” said Blathers, nodding agreement and idly rattling the handcuffs as though they were castanets. “Who is this boy? What story does he tell about himself? Where's he come from? He didn't fall out of the clouds, did he, master?”

“Certainly not,” replied the doctor, casting a nervous look toward the two ladies. “I know his entire history, but we can discuss it in a little while. First, I imagine, you'd wish to examine the spot where the thieves tried to enter?”

“Certainly,” Mr. Blathers answered. “Best inspect the premises first and question the servants afterward. That's the proper order of business.”

Lights were fetched. Messrs. Blathers and Duff, accompanied by the local constable, Brittles, Giles, and, in short, everybody else, entered the little room at the passage's end and peered out of the window. Next they went around across the lawn and peered in through it. Then they had a candle passed out to examine the shutter, followed by a lantern to follow the footprints, and finally a pitchfork to probe the bushes. Having accomplished all this under the breathlessly interested eyes of the onlookers, they returned indoors. Mr. Giles and Brittles were then required to give a melodramatic performance of their parts in the previous night's adventures. They repeated it some six times, differing on no more than one important point at the first telling and no more than a dozen at the last. Once this satisfactory conclusion was reached, Blathers and Duff emptied the room and held a lengthy conference. Beside its secrecy and solemnity, a consultation among eminent doctors on medicine's most difficult problem would have seemed mere children's play.

Meanwhile, in the adjoining room, the doctor paced in considerable distress, while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched with anxious expressions.

“Upon my word,” he said, stopping after a great many rapid turns, “I scarcely know what to do.”
